4 SKILLS

Four skills, from easy to hard

Every question tests one of these. Knowing which one tells you what kind of answer to expect.

L1 · Stated facts

Times, places, numbers, names.

“The train leaves at 9:15.”

L2 · Opinions

How someone feels, in opinion words.

“Honestly, it was a waste of money.”

L3 · Connections

Linking two ideas: cause, effect, contrast.

“Because the buses stopped, she walked.”

L4 · Implied meaning

The answer is never said. You work it out.

“Well… I suppose the seats were comfortable.”

Key
24 of the 40 marks involve L4 — Exercises 2, 4 and 5. Listening only for stated facts plays for about 16 marks.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening4
4 minThe intellectual spine of the workshop. Do not read the notes — say each example sentence and ask which skill it tests. The number that changes how they listen: L4 is tested in Exercises 2, 4 and 5 — 24 of the 40 marks. A student hunting only stated facts caps out around 16. Do not overstate it: in an L4 question the answer is present, just never in the option's words. That is exactly why the next slides matter.

THE METHOD

T.A.C.O. — four beats, every question

– possible answer ✗ sure it is wrong ✓ the answer
Put a small pencil dash (–)

next to a possible answer on hearing 1. Nothing is final yet.

Draw a cross (✗)

next to any choice you know for sure is wrong.

Then ask: which option is the trap?

The distractor is in the audio on purpose. Name it before you choose.

Why
Free marks are won at T — before the audio starts.

Steps!

  1. T — Target: read the question and all the options.
  2. A — Attend: hearing 1, get the topic. Dash a possible answer.
  3. C — Confirm: hearing 2, decide. Which option is the trap?
  4. O — Output: circle one letter. Never leave a blank.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening7
4 minMake it physical. Everyone holds up a pen and shows a dash versus a cross versus a circle. If they cannot tell them apart on the page they will not know whether they have committed. The most common failure is skipping T: listening with unread options, hearing one familiar word, locking it in. That is how the paper is designed to catch them. The three instructions on this slide are the marking habits for the whole workshop — dash, cross, then hunt the trap. We reuse these symbols on every worked question.
TWO HEARINGS

Hearing 1 and hearing 2 are different jobs

Hearing 1Hearing 2
Your jobUnderstand the whole recordingDecide each answer
Your penA small dash (tick ✓) by a possible answerA firm circle round the final letter
Your eyesMostly on the question paperMostly listening
NeverLock an answer inRe-read every option
Listen for
not · never · only · already · instead · unless · but · actually · in the end

To do!

  1. Hearing 1: understand the whole recording.
  2. Put a small dash (tick ✓) by a possible answer — not a circle.
  3. Hearing 2: decide. Circle the final letter.
  4. Never re-read every option on hearing 2.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening8
3 minThe highest-value behaviour change in the workshop. Most mid-band candidates use hearing 1 to answer and hearing 2 to check they were right — so hearing 2 does no new work. Teach the split: hearing 1 builds the map, hearing 2 plants the flag. The pen line is the physical version of that: a dash first, a circle second. Write the flip-words on the board: not, never, only, already, instead, unless, but, actually, in the end. In the real 2025 paper these decide Question 1, Question 6 and Question 13.

Part two

Exercise by exercise

October / November 2025  ·  Variant __VAR__

—Section divider. Tell them the pattern: for each exercise they see a real question, get the real reading time, and commit to an answer before we look at the audio script together. The variant number here comes from the same VARIANT constant as slide 1.
EXERCISE 1

One picture question each: eight short extracts with 4 visual options.

Careful
Exercise 1 has no reading pause. Skim all eight questions before the exam audio begins.

Steps!

  1. Read the four pictures first.
  2. Name what changes from A to D.
  3. Listen for that one change.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening11
3 minBoth images are from the real paper. Let them look at Question 1 now; you will use it properly on the next two slides. The structural fact to say: Exercise 1 has no reading pause — only three seconds before Question 1. So skim all eight Exercise 1 questions before the exam audio starts at all, during the instructions.
EXERCISE 1

Four visual options of four different settings for a question.

Ask: what single thing changes from A to B to C to D?

In Question 1 it is where the car is parked. Nothing else matters.

Place options

car park · station · petrol station · supermarket

Time options

o'clock · half past · quarter to · delayed · brought forward

Watch out
When two pictures look almost the same, the answer is one of those two. That is where the decision is.

Steps!

  1. Find the one thing that changes.
  2. Predict the words you will hear.
  3. Spot the two pictures that look almost the same.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening12
3 minThe core insight: four pictures are one idea at four settings. Make them practise naming the axis out loud on Question 1 — the answer is "where the car is". Then pre-loading: if the options are places, the words car park, station, petrol station, supermarket should be in their head before the audio starts. Recognition beats comprehension under time pressure. The near-duplicate rule is reliable: if two options are almost identical, the discrimination is between them.
QUESTION 1

Question 1 — you have 3 seconds

Play Question 1
The real recording, played twice
--:--
The audio says
“there wasn't a single space left in the pool car park… I hope you didn't leave it at the train station like last time… It's actually next to the petrol station… the supermarket's nearer… but I'd feel bad parking there without doing any shopping!”
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening13
4 minRun it properly. Give them ten seconds, and make everyone write a letter before you reveal anything. Then press R. Most classes split between A, B and D — which is the perfect teaching moment, because three of the four pictures are mentioned: D train station is a past mistake; B supermarket is considered and refused; C pond is never mentioned; A petrol station is the only one that is true. The rule: the answer is what is true at the END of the extract, not what is said during it.
QUESTION 1

Why A is right — and how the other three are built

Every card below is one option of Question 1. The label tells you its job.

Girl: How was swimming club?  Dad: Great, but I'm pretty tired.
Dad: …there wasn't a single space left in the pool car park.
Girl: I hope you didn't leave it at the train station like last time.
Dad: I'll never make that mistake again! It's actually next to the petrol station.
Girl: …but the supermarket's nearer.  Dad: Yes, but I'd feel bad parking there.
A · ANSWER

“It's actually next to the petrol station.” True at the end.

B · TRAP

Suggested by the girl — and refused: “but I'd feel bad…”

C · TRAP

Never said. It exists only to fill the fourth box.

D · TRAP

A past mistake: “like last time… never again.”

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening14
4 minThis slide used to be confusing because the cards were only labelled A–D with no indication of which option they referred to. Now each card carries a letter label plus its role — ANSWER or TRAP — and the subtitle says explicitly that each card is one option of Question 1. Walk the extract and name the trap as you go: B is the rejected suggestion, C is the never-mentioned option, D is the past mistake, and the answer is signalled by “actually” — one of the flip-words. Have them underline “actually” in their own copy. The transferable rule for the rule box: in Exercise 1, the answer is true at the end of the extract.
EXERCISE 1

Four traps, and one rule that beats them all

1 · A number that gets cancelled

“It was going to be ten… no, half past nine.”

2 · The past plan

“I used to park there.” Old information.

3 · The mentioned picture

Shown, then rejected — or a past mistake.

4 · The near-miss pair

Two options differ by a tiny detail. Both get said.

The rule
Ask on every item: “Is this still true at the end?”

To do!

  1. Wait for the sentence to finish.
  2. Ask: is this still true at the end?
  3. If it was mentioned and then changed, cross it.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening15
3 minThese four traps are one idea wearing different clothes, and the rule at the bottom is the whole of Exercise 1: is this still true at the end? Practise it immediately on Question 1: the supermarket was mentioned then refused, so it fails the test. Homework: do Questions 2 to 8 and write beside each wrong picture the reason — rejected, past plan, never said or near-miss. That labelling is worth more than the mark.
EXERCISE 2

Five extracts. Two questions each. Best value on the paper.

GOLDEN RULE

  • The correct option re-words the audio. The traps repeat it.

Steps!

  1. Read both questions in the 15-second pause.
  2. Label each one F (fact) or S (stance).
  3. One recording answers both — so losing it costs two marks.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening16
3 minTwo facts: 10 marks for five extracts — the best value on the paper; and because two questions come from one recording, one moment of inattention costs two marks. The 15-second pause before every pair is the gift here — enough to read two questions and three options each, if you are not staring at the ceiling. Read the GOLDEN RULE aloud. We will prove it on Questions 9 and 10.
EXERCISE 2

The two questions usually do different jobs

F · FACT

How…? Where…? What kind…? The answer is stated. Usually winnable on hearing 1.

S · STANCE

Why…? How does she feel…? An opinion or reason — and the option is worded differently.

Do this
Write F or S in the pause, so you can see at a glance which one is still unanswered.
Careful
A strong habit, not a rule. Sometimes both are facts. Use it to aim your attention.

Steps!

  1. Write F or S beside each question.
  2. Hearing 1: get the fact.
  3. Hearing 2: decide the stance.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening17
3 minBe honest that this is a tendency, not a published rule — students who treat it as a rule get caught. What is reliable is the distinction: some questions are answered by a stated fact, others by a stance. Writing F or S next to each question turns a vague instruction into a visible checklist they can glance at mid-recording. Demonstrate on Questions 9 and 10 (next slide): Q9 "How did the boy learn…" is a fact; Q10 "What made the boy choose…" is a reason — a stance.
QUESTIONS 9–10

Questions 9 and 10 — 15 seconds

Play Questions 9 and 10
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Boy: There are literally thousands of websites and film clips on the internet, each of which contains someone guiding you step-by-step. Attending classes was totally unnecessary.

So why the environment? Unlike many students, I'd only developed a passion relatively recently, but I realised there were a vast number of issues within a single subject, so each video could be different. My marks have improved as a result.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening18
5 minGive them 15 seconds with a real timer, then a letter for each question. Then press R. Q9 = A (online resources) — “thousands of websites… guiding you step-by-step”. Trap C the short course is killed by “totally unnecessary”. Q10 = C (many different aspects) — “a vast number of issues… each video could be different”. The traps are the star. A long-term interest is contradicted by “only… relatively recently”. And B is the cleverest trap so far: his marks did improve — but as a consequence, not the reason, and nobody suggested it. That is a reversed cause-and-effect trap.
QUESTIONS 13–14

Questions 13 and 14 — another pair

Play Questions 13 and 14
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Girl: Have you been to that new café?  Boy: I felt totally at home there.
Girl: Like your favourite relative's house. But more choice of things to eat'd make it better.
Boy: I'm so pleased it's open in the evening.  Girl: It'd be great before school too — shame it's shut then.
Girl: I might ask if they have any jobs.  Boy: I can imagine you chatting with the customers.
Girl: I meant in the kitchen. I'm hoping to do a catering course — valuable experience.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening19
6 min15 seconds, commit, then reveal. Q13 = C (welcoming) — “totally at home”, “favourite relative's house”. Q14 = B (career aims) — “catering course… valuable experience”. Three traps to name. A opening hours is a polarity flip — “shame it's shut” before school. B wide variety of food is a criticism, not a fact — she asks for MORE choice. And the best one: C “she would meet lots of people” comes from the boy and the girl corrects him — “I meant in the kitchen.” That is a wrong-speaker trap inside Exercise 2. Highlight the correction and say it: when one speaker corrects the other, the correction is the answer.
EXERCISE 2

The correct option re-words. The traps repeat.

IMPORTANT!

  • A familiar word is bait, not proof.
If an option copies the audio…

…be suspicious. Recognising your own word feels safe — that feeling is the trap.

If an option re-words it…

…it is often the answer. Four moves: synonym · idiom · polarity flip · cause/effect flip.

Keep one list

Audio words on the left, option words on the right. Ten per paper.

To do!

  1. Hear an option’s exact words? Be suspicious.
  2. Find the option that says the same idea differently.
  3. Write the pair in your paraphrase list.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening20
3 minTeach the emotional flip: right now, recognising a word makes you feel safe. We want it to make you suspicious. Then the caveat: for pure factual questions the answer can be word-for-word (Question 1's “petrol station” was literal). So this is a check, not the decision. The paraphrase list is the best homework in the workshop: two columns, ten entries per paper. That is a personal dictionary of the moves Cambridge actually uses.
EXERCISE 3

One talk. Eight gaps to fill.

Good news
Exercise 3 tests stated facts and opinions only — no implied meaning. The cheapest 8 marks on the paper.

Steps!

  1. Read all eight sentences in the 40 seconds.
  2. Underline the word before each gap.
  3. The questions follow the order of the talk.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening21
3 minExercise 3 is the other cheap exercise: L1 to L3 only, no L4. A drilled class should bank 7 or 8 and any loss is a technique problem. Point at the 40 seconds in the Steps box — eight questions, about five seconds each. The questions run in the same order as the talk, so they act as a map of the monologue. Have them look at Questions 19 to 21 and notice: every one offers three numbers. That is a warning about what is coming.
EXERCISE 3

Use the sentence to cross out wrong options

You can often dismiss an option before you hear a single word.

1 · What kind of word?

“…on the site of an old ___” → a singular noun.

2 · Which way?

“The biggest problem was ___” → something negative.

3 · Can it decide?

“about ___ million years ago” → 200, 250, 400 all fit.

Question 19: The oldest shark species living today appeared about ___ million years ago.   A 200   B 250   C 400
All three are numbers, so all three fit. Do not guess — write # in the margin and match each number to its fact.

Steps!

  1. What kind of word fits the gap?
  2. Which way does the sentence point?
  3. If all three fit, only the audio can decide.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening22
4 minOne message: the sentence itself can eliminate options. Walk the three questions and give ten seconds after each. Be honest about step 3 — that is the part students get wrong. For Q19 all three numbers fit and all three are said, so the sentence cannot decide it. Students taught that this trick always works lose confidence the first time it does not. What IS reliable: word class and direction. And when all three fit, write # in the margin and match numbers to facts.
EXERCISE 3

In the margin: symbols, not words

Before the audio: number your margin 1–8

+   −   ?   X   →   BUT   #

+ good news  ·  − bad news  ·  ? not sure  ·  X ruled out  ·  → cause and effect  ·  # a number was said

Not this
Writing words or full sentences. Every word written is a second not listening.
This
One symbol per question. On hearing 2 you look at your symbols.
If you fall behind
Do not go back to the question you missed. Stay with the recording — find the next question number and rejoin there.

Steps!

  1. Number your margin 1–8 before the audio.
  2. Write one symbol per question on hearing 1.
  3. Hearing 2: go back to the ones marked ? or X.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening23
3 minExercise 3 is where students run out of working memory. Eight questions and one long talk is more than you can hold, so you write a skeleton instead. Make them do it physically: number the margin 1 to 8 now, then copy the symbols. Physically doing it once beats describing it five times. The two most useful symbols are # (a number or price was said) and BUT (a contradiction is coming). The recovery rule is the one that saves marks: do not go back; stay with the recording.
QUESTIONS 19–21

Questions 19, 20, 21 — three numbers each

Play the shark talk
Questions 19 to 21
--:--
Several types still found swimming in our oceans have done so for almost 200 million years. Their ancestors emerged around 400 million years ago, but most disappeared just over 250 million years ago.

Before the sixteenth century the term ‘sea dog’ described the large fish sailors spotted. A Dutch word — shurck — roughly meaning ‘bad person’ is the likely source.

The largest group is made up of just under 300 species, so well over half of the 500 or so varieties in our seas. Of this total, around 450 live close to the shore.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening24
6 minThe best number-training exercise in the paper: all three questions offer three numbers and the audio says all three. Give 40 seconds, then reveal. Q19 = A (200) — “still found swimming… almost 200 million”. Traps: 400 (the ancestors) and 250 (when most disappeared). Q20 = A (bad person) — shurck. Traps: sea dog (the previous word) and large fish (what sea dog described). Q21 = C (500) — “500 or so varieties”. Traps: 300 (only the largest group) and 450 (only those near the shore). State the rule: every number belongs to something. Match the number to the question — do not just hear a number.
EXERCISE 4

Six speakers. Eight statements. Two are never used.

IMPORTANT!

  • A letter is only used once. Two letters are left over.

Steps!

  1. Read all eight statements in the 30 seconds.
  2. Write a 2–3 word label beside each.
  3. Match the whole idea, not one keyword.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening25
4 minRead the instruction box with them: “Use each letter only once. There are two extra letters which you do not need to use.” So six speakers, eight statements, two left over. Then read A to H together and notice how similar some are: A, E and G are all about how the speaker felt; B, D and H are all reactions. Several pairs share a topic but point in different directions — that is the design.
EXERCISE 4

Six speakers plus eight statements is too much to remember

Before speaker 1 — write this in the margin

A ___   B ___   C ___   D ___

E ___   F ___   G ___   H ___

When speaker 2 matches F…

write 2 beside F. Cross the letter out.

A letter is only used once.

If two speakers point at F, you have made a mistake.

Why
The count is a free error detector. Most Exercise 4 mistakes are a statement used twice without noticing.

Steps!

  1. Write A–H down the margin before speaker 1.
  2. Write the speaker number beside the letter you use.
  3. At the end: 6 used, 2 left over.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening26
3 minMake them build the ledger in their own margin now. Physically doing it once beats describing it five times. The core insight: Exercise 4 is a working-memory problem, not an English problem. Six speakers plus eight statements is fourteen items — more than anyone holds reliably. The count is the part students never think of: six speakers must consume six different letters, with two left over. And: never leave a speaker blank.
SPEAKERS 1–2

Speakers 1 and 2 — which statement fits?

Statements A–H are on the previous slide. You have 30 seconds.

Play Speakers 1 and 2
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Speaker 1: I thought it'd be the first and last time, but my performance showed enough promise to have another go. I'm astonished it went so well — the first competitor sang my song, so I rapidly decided to switch my choice of music.

Speaker 2: Considering I spent every spare minute practising, I would've been amazed if I'd finished last. The people watching were mainly parents, so it's hardly surprising they clapped everyone so enthusiastically.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening27
6 min30 seconds, commit. Q27 = E (changed my mind about what to perform) — “decided to switch my choice of music”. Q28 = C (prepared as well as I could) — “spent every spare minute practising”. Now the real work: how many statements are built from the speaker's own words and then reversed. Speaker 1: A (“never enter another one”) undone by “enough promise to have another go”; G (“never felt so nervous”) undone because the anxiety was reduced. Speaker 2: D (“sure I was going to come last”) is the exact reversal — he would have been amazed to finish last. H undone by “hardly surprising”. Ask them to name the flip-words: but, hardly, reduced, never again.
EXERCISE 5

One interview. Eight questions. One speaker who counts.

IMPORTANT!

  • The answers come from the main speaker only — not the interviewer.

Steps!

  1. Decide which voice is the main speaker.
  2. Mark it on your paper.
  3. Read all eight questions in the 45 seconds.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening28
4 minRead the instruction line: “You will hear an interview with a competitive skateboarder called Mikaela Quayle.” Then the key sentence from the syllabus — the questions test information expressed by the main speaker. Define “main speaker” operationally: the person being interviewed, the one who answers. The interviewer is scaffolding. That gives the habit: before you hear a word, decide which voice counts and mark it on your paper. Flag the 45 seconds — the longest reading pause in the paper, because there are eight questions.
EXERCISE 5

Ask “who said it?” before “is it true?”

The interviewer is a trap factory

The interviewer asks, guesses and summarises — and those become wrong options.

“So it was all about the charity, then?”
“You must have been exhausted?”

Wait for the correction

When the main speaker disagrees, the correction is the answer.

not exactly · well, not quite · I meant…

The habit
Tag every opinion in your head: INT says… or MAIN says…. It removes the most common Exercise 5 error.

Steps!

  1. Tag every opinion: INT or MAIN.
  2. Distrust anything the interviewer states.
  3. Wait for the main speaker’s correction.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening29
3 minAttribution is the Exercise 5 skill. Name it and make it a habit: mentally prefix every opinion with INT or MAIN. Two versions: the interviewer's guess becomes a wrong option (“You must have been exhausted?”) — it sounds like a description but it is a question; and the interviewer's summary becomes a wrong option which the main speaker rebuts. Give them the correction markers: not exactly, well not quite, that's not how I'd put it, I meant. Point back: this trap already appeared in Exercise 2 — “I meant in the kitchen.”
QUESTIONS 33–34

Questions 33 and 34 — the interview begins

Play Questions 33 and 34
The interview begins here
--:--
Interviewer: How did it start?
Mikaela: I was learning to walk and Dad noticed I hardly ever fell over. As a skateboarder himself, he said, ‘Let's put her on a skateboard' — I was eighteen months old! I've no memory of that, but I was never without my skateboard.

When I was three, Dad took me to the skateboard park. I didn't necessarily admire the older skaters. I wanted to try tricks, and was shocked when I realised how hard it was.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening30
6 min45 seconds of reading time, then commit. Q33 = C (forgotten getting on a skateboard) — “I've no memory of that”. Q34 = B (surprised by the challenges) — “I was shocked when I realised how hard it was”; shocked re-worded as surprised. The traps are worth more than the answers. Q33 A (“refused any other transport”) is a degree shift — she was “never without” it. Q33 B (“satisfy her father's dreams”) is an invented motive; it was Dad's idea, but nothing about her hopes. Q34 C is directly negated: “didn't necessarily admire”.
EXERCISE 5

The words that give away an opinion

L2 and L4 questions are won or lost on these. Each column does a different job.

Column 1

An opinion is coming

to be honest · if I'm honest · I'd say · frankly · I must admit

Do: get ready — the answer is next.

Column 2

The meaning flips

but · however · although · actually · that said · hardly

Do: cross out what came before.

Column 3

A feeling, no feeling word

it grew on me · I could take it or leave it · it left me cold · it fell flat

Do: learn what each one means.

Build one page
Add every new phrase you meet to one page. Worth more than another practice paper.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening31
4 minThis is a signal slide, not a vocabulary list. Teach the three columns as three separate instructions. Column 1: demonstrate it live — say “if I'm honest, …” and have the class say “here it comes” back. Column 2 is the highest-value family in the paper: everything before but / however / actually is the decoy. Prove it from questions they have seen: Q1 (“actually”), Q13 (“shame it's shut”), Q10 (“improved as a result” — consequence, not reason). Column 3 is a finite vocabulary job: “it left me cold”, “it fell flat” are exactly the hedged evaluations that options paraphrase into “she was disappointed”.
Part three

Using the transcript

The answer key for everything you practised.

1 minSet up the section. Most students finish a past paper, check the score and put it away — which wastes the paper. The transcript shows you exactly which words decided each answer, and it is the only way to find out whether a mistake was a mishearing or a wrong decision. A paper you do not review teaches you almost nothing, because you simply rehearse your existing habits.
REVIEW

A paper without a review is a wasted paper

What most students do

  • Do the paper, count the score, close the file.
  • Say “I misheard it” and move on.
  • Repeat the same mistakes next time.
  • Never find out which word suggested the answer.

What raises your score

  • Do the paper, then refer to the transcript.
  • Find the exact phrase that earns each mark.
  • Identify the trap that caught you.
  • Add the wording to your paraphrase list.
Rule
A mistake you have diagnosed is worth marks next time. One reviewed paper beats three unreviewed ones.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening33
3 minThe key line: one reviewed paper beats three unreviewed ones. Students default to volume; we want diagnosis. Ban the phrase “I misheard it”. It is not diagnostic and leads to no change. Instead they must identify the reason: cancelled number, past plan, rejected suggestion, wrong speaker, polarity flip, degree shift, never said. Show the arithmetic: lose six marks a paper and diagnose only two, and the other four repeat all year.
THE TRANSCRIPT

Four things to look for on every page

R1  Question 1
Where did the girl's dad park their car?
PAUSE 00'03"
M: male, forties, UK accent
F: female, mid-teens, UK accent
M: How was swimming club?
F: Great, but I'm pretty tired.
[ end of extract ]
PAUSE 00'05"
REPEAT FROM * TO **
1 · M: and F:

Each line is labelled — you can check who said it.

2 · Voice descriptions

“male, forties” tells you which voice is which.

3 · Every PAUSE

The gap is where you commit your answer.

4 · REPEAT FROM * TO **

Shows exactly which part is played twice.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening34
4 minHand out the transcript and look at the real thing together. Walk the four features. The most useful is number 1: because the transcript marks M and F line by line, you can prove to a student that their wrong answer came from the other speaker — which is the whole of the Exercise 5 technique made visible. It is also how you demonstrate Question 14: the boy says “chatting with the customers”, the girl says “I meant in the kitchen”. Point out that the transcript records the PAUSE times, which is how we know the reading times are 15, 40, 30 and 45 seconds. Practical tip: the transcript is a teacher document — give it to students after they have attempted the questions.
THE DRILL

How to review a paper in twenty minutes

Step 1 · Do it properly first

Full speed, one play, no pausing. Write the answer for all 40 — including guesses.

Step 2 · Mark it, but do not look at the answers

Just look at which questions were wrong.

Step 3 · Now refer to the transcript

For each wrong question, underline the phrase that earns the mark — then identify the trap.

Step 4 · Replay only those extracts

Listen again with the script in front of you. Your ear connects the written phrase to the sound.

Write this
rejected suggestion · past plan · never said · wrong speaker · polarity flip · degree shift · number for something else

Steps!

  1. Do it properly first: full speed, one play, no pausing. Write the answer for all 40 — including guesses.
  2. Mark it, but do not look at the answers yet.
  3. Now refer to the transcript. Underline the phrase that earns the mark.
  4. Replay only those extracts.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening35
3 minThe method you want them to use at home, so keep it concrete and time-boxed. Step 3 must not be skipped — underline the phrase, identify the trap. Step 2 matters more than it looks: mark it without reading the answers first, or reviewing becomes reading rather than diagnosing. Step 4 is where weaker listeners learn most: hearing the phrase while looking at it written is what connects sound to words. Set this as the standing homework for every practice paper, and give the trap-name list at the bottom as the vocabulary they must use.
Part four

Exam craft

The six minutes that decide your paper.

1 minSignal the shift: everything so far was about listening; this part is about the mechanics of the exam room, where marks are lost for reasons that have nothing to do with English.
EXAM CRAFT

Forty answers. Six minutes. Do not lose them here.

Time! 5:00 transfer
Time! 1:00 final check
The three silent disasters

Off by one. All your answers are correct, but every one is written on the wrong line.

Double-shaded. Two letters on one line.

Blank line. A blank is worth zero for certain.

Check
Count the lines as you finish. If your final answer is on line 40, your transfer is almost certainly right.

Steps!

  1. Transfer in blocks of five.
  2. Cover the lines below with your hand.
  3. Sweep at the end: no blanks, no doubles.
  4. Your last answer must be on line 40.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening37
4 minDo this physically if you can — hand out a real answer sheet and have them shade five blocks while covering the lines below with their hand. Three minutes, and it removes a whole category of loss. The numbers are real: the transcript shows a five-minute pause then a further one-minute pause. About nine seconds per line — the risk is not time, it is mechanical error. The count check is arithmetic they already trust: 8 + 10 + 8 + 6 + 8 = 40. Last answer on line 40 = aligned; on line 39 = a line was skipped and there is still time to find it. Say the unpopular thing: a blank line is a certain zero.
EXAM CRAFT

Eight mistakes that cost marks every year

1 · Not reading the options

Listening to an unread question.

2 · Choosing what you recognise

A familiar word is bait.

3 · Missing the “but”

Everything before the pivot is the decoy.

4 · Answering from the interviewer

Right idea, wrong speaker.

5 · Re-reading everything on hearing 2

Narrow to your two candidates.

6 · Chasing a lost question

Jump to the next number.

7 · Writing words in the margin

Symbols only.

8 · Leaving a blank

A guess sometimes scores.

To do!

  1. Write your two worst mistakes on your paper.
  2. Tick them off at the end of the paper.
  3. Fix one habit at a time.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening38
3 minDo not read all eight aloud. Ask instead: “put your hand up if number 3 sounds like you… number 1?… number 8?” The same three or four attract almost everybody — the losses are clustered and predictable. Then set the ritual: each student writes their own two worst mistakes on the front of every practice paper, and ticks them off at the end. Trivial, and it works. If you only fix one, fix number 1.
FROM TODAY

A four-week plan

WEEK 1

Find your pattern

One paper, then review with the transcript. Identify every trap. Start your paraphrase page.

WEEK 2

Fix Ex 1 and 3

Questions 1–8 and 19–26 of two papers. Label every wrong picture.

WEEK 3

Attack 2, 4 and 5

One full paper. Re-do only Exercises 2, 4, 5 with the transcript. Quote the phrase.

WEEK 4

Rehearse it

Two timed papers with a real answer sheet. No new words — technique only.

The rule
Never do a paper without reviewing it. An hour of review is worth three papers of practice.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening39
3 minPresent it as four focuses rather than four calendar weeks — adapt freely. The discipline is the rule at the bottom: never do a paper without reviewing it. Week 2 targets the cheap marks (Exercises 1 and 3, 16 marks, L1–L3 only); the milestone is Exercise 1 at 7–8 out of 8. Week 3 targets the 24-mark block and its discipline is the licensing quote: no quote, no mark. Week 4 is rehearsal only, including the transfer on a real answer sheet. No new vocabulary in the last week.
BE HONEST

Six things to be able to say yes to

Tick only the ones that are true under exam conditions — not when you are relaxed.

1. I read all the options during the pause, every time.
2. I dash on hearing 1 and circle on hearing 2 — never the same job twice.
3. I can identify what caught me: rejected, past plan, wrong speaker, polarity flip.
4. In Exercise 4 I build the A–H ledger before speaker 1.
5. In Exercise 5 I ask who said it? before is it true?
6. I never leave a blank, and I have never been off by one.
Scoring
5–6 yes: your technique is ready.  3–4: pick your two weakest for three weeks.  0–2: fix the routine before doing more papers.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening40
3 minHave them tick honestly in pencil and count. The scoring bands normalise the middle: most strong candidates land at 3 or 4, and that is a target list, not a failure. Each statement maps to a slide, so a student can self-serve: 1 → the reading-times slide; 2 → two hearings; 3 → the trap slides; 4 → the Exercise 4 ledger; 5 → Exercise 5 attribution; 6 → the transfer slide. The 0–2 band matters most: more papers will not help. The routine has to change first.
REMEMBER

Six things to remember

Read before you listen

The paper gives you 15, 30, 40 and 45 seconds.

Two hearings, two jobs

Hearing 1 maps it. Hearing 2 decides it.

Distrust what you recognise

The answer re-words. The trap repeats.

Hunt the pivot

but · however · actually · not · hardly.

Ask who said it

The interviewer is a trap factory.

Review with the transcript

One diagnosed paper beats three.

Remember
Paper 2 is not mainly a test of how much English you know. It is a test of how well you handle a recording you only hear twice.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE ESL 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening41
3 minDo not re-teach this — use it as a retrieval quiz. Cover the slide, read out the six headings one at a time, and ask the class to recall the detail before you reveal it. The closing framing is genuinely liberating for a strong class: you already have the English. What separates a 26 from a 34 at this level is the routine. One sentence to leave with: read before you listen, decide on the second hearing, distrust the words you recognise, and never leave a blank.

All the best!
